title: LDSCI6253 Week 4 · The Power of Colour

slides.name: 1 · The Power of Colour

params.text: LDSCI6253 Advanced Information Presentation & Visualisation · Week 4
LDSCI6253 WEEK 4 · THE POWER OF COLOUR

slides.notes:
Up as they arrive.
The question for the whole session: why does colour matter so much in data visualisation? By the end they should be able to answer it in their own words.

slides.name: 2 · Before we start

params.text: Munzner, Visualization Analysis and Design, Chapter 10: Map Color and Other Channels
On Canvas by midday on the Friday after the lab
Ask early. Don’t wait until the last minute
Plan the week, not the night before

slides.notes:
1 min. Week 2 promised "Week 4 is a whole lecture on colour". This is it.
READING. The 2025 deck listed Chapters 4 and 10. Chapter 4 is validation; Chapter 10 is the colour chapter. The course overview lists 10–12. Decide before teaching (plan §9, D1).

slides.name: 3 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
2 min across seven clicks. Each click lights one stage and dims the rest; the last click lights them all.
1 Raw data: 366 lines, a date and a count. 2 Table: items in rows, attributes in columns. 3 Types: Month and Day are ordinal and cyclic; Hires is quantitative. 4 The question decides the task: find the peak. 5 The visualisation: a heatmap, and its colour is today’s subject. 6 The insight the reader leaves with.
SAY: "Last week we classified attributes as categorical, ordinal or quantitative. Today you’ll see why that matters: the attribute type decides which colour map you’re allowed to use. Hires is quantitative, so it gets a lightness ramp: darker means more."
Munzner’s nested model sits behind it: domain → abstraction → idiom → algorithm. Fix carried over: the 2025 deck spelt the name "Manzner".
Data: mean hires per day by month and weekday, 2024, from lessons/tfl-daily-cycle-hires.xlsx (TfL / London Datastore).

slides.name: 10 · Full picture
slides.notes:
5 min. WHY: slide 3 ends at "pick the chart", and students struggle to get from data types to a chart choice (pie or bar, line or scatter). WHAT: a 5-minute explainer in three signposts. WHAT: items, attributes and N, O, Q, and is it time? WHY: action plus target. HOW: the channel ranking, then expressive and effective. It then tests both questions on the Lab 1 TfL 2024 file. HOW: play it straight through; it ends on four new scenarios.
HANDS UP on the end card, then ask for the reason. 1 Week split (4 parts, sums to 100%): a pie can work, a 100% stacked bar compares better. 2 Rent in eight boroughs: a sorted bar. 3 Temperature across October: a line, because days are a sequence. 4 Hours against mark: a scatter, because each dot is a pair of measures with no order.
Every bar and dot is plotted from the real file. Average hire time is the file’s mean per month.

slides.name: 11 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
4 min across five clicks. WHY: this is the shortcut students meet everywhere (chart choosers, the FT Visual Vocabulary): name the purpose, get a chart family. WHAT: four purposes, each on the same TfL 2024 data, so only the question changes. HOW: one card per click, then all four; ask the room to name the chart before you reveal the next card.
1 COMPARISON. "Which month was busiest?" Twelve categories, one number each: a bar chart, because length on a shared baseline is the second-best channel. July, just ahead of August and June.

args.caption: Pick the chart by its purpose
args.credit: Comparison, part of a whole, trend over time, relationship

slides.name: 12 · Framed picture
slides.notes: 2 PART OF A WHOLE. "What share were weekday hires?" Three parts that sum to 100%: a pie can do it (76% weekday). The test from the video: 2–5 parts and a real 100%. With more parts, or to compare shares across years, use a 100% stacked bar.

args.caption: Pick the chart by its purpose
args.credit: Comparison, part of a whole, trend over time, relationship

slides.name: 13 · Framed picture
slides.notes: 3 TREND OVER TIME. "How did hires change through 2024?" Months are ordered and each leads to the next, so a line: the line itself says "this continues into that". Peak in July, low in December.

args.caption: Pick the chart by its purpose
args.credit: Comparison, part of a whole, trend over time, relationship

slides.name: 14 · Framed picture
slides.notes: 4 RELATIONSHIP. "Do busier months mean longer rides?" Two numbers for each month: a scatter. Position on two axes shows whether they move together (they do: about 15 minutes in winter, 19 in summer). Joining these dots would invent an order.

args.caption: Pick the chart by its purpose
args.credit: Comparison, part of a whole, trend over time, relationship

slides.name: 15 · Framed picture
slides.notes: All four. SAY: "The purpose names the family; the data types confirm it." ASK: "A table of exam marks and hours studied for 60 students: which card?" (relationship, scatter). Warn that the shortcut breaks when the purpose is vague, so ask what the reader must do first. Average hire time is the file’s monthly mean.

slides.name: 16 · By the end of today you can

params.text: By the end of today you can
how your eyes turn light into colour, and why colour is always relative
hue, lightness and saturation, and which suits which data
a sequential, diverging or categorical colour map, and justify it
a chart’s colour, including who it shuts out
an accessible colour scale in Altair, and test it

slides.notes:
1 min.
SAY: "Outcome 4 is what you’ll do in the next five minutes, badly, and in the last ten minutes, well."

slides.name: 17 · Case A · What is colour doing here?

params.text: Case A · What is colour doing here?

Red, yellow, green and tan are political-map colours. They encode no data.

Red reads as danger or alarm, yet it is handed out at random.

The numbers do all the work; colour adds noise, and implies groups that aren’t there.

Raw counts, not normalised by population: not a colour problem, but a choropleth problem.

slides.notes:
2.5 min. ASK first, collect the cloud, then flip (⇄) for the points.
Expect "nothing", "decoration", "countries". The lesson: colour that means nothing still says something.
Source: 2025 Week 4 deck p6.

args.caption: Case A · What is colour doing here?
args.credit: US ancestry by European country · ACS 2019
args.facts:

Red reads as danger or alarm, yet it is handed out at random.
The numbers do all the work; colour adds noise, and implies groups that aren’t there.

slides.name: 18 · Case B · What is colour doing here?

params.text: Case B · What is colour doing here?

The sequential blue matches the blue sea: data and basemap share a hue.

The lightest classes melt into the pale land.

The legend labels only its ends, 12% and 31%.

Is a white country “no data” or “low”? The map can’t say.

slides.notes:
2.5 min. Hands up, then flip.
ASK: "Spain is white. Low profit, or no data?" Nobody can answer, which is the point.
Source: 2025 Week 4 deck p7.

args.caption: Case B · What is colour doing here?
args.credit: Most profitable markets, percentage of goods sold

slides.name: 19 · Case C · What is colour doing here?

params.text: Case C · What is colour doing here?

The data are ordered age bins; the colours are unordered rainbow hues.

Red (29–31) and purple (over 31) are hard to tell apart, and purple wraps back towards blue.

Bubble size and position mean nothing.

“Parantel” for parental: check the small things too.

slides.notes:
2 min.
ASK: "Which colour means oldest? How did you know?" They had to read the legend, because hue has no order.
Source: 2025 Week 4 deck p8.

slides.name: 20 · Full picture

params.text: Park them. We fix all three at the end.
You could tell something was wrong before you could say why

slides.notes:
30 s.
SAY: "Notice that you could tell something was wrong before you could say why. Today is about building the vocabulary for the why." They come back in the last section.

slides.name: 21 · Section · What does colour do for your eye?

params.text: What does colour do for your eye?

slides.notes: 20 s. Before any theory: three quick experiments on the room.

slides.name: 22 · Full picture
slides.notes:
45 s. Say nothing; count three in your head, then click.
SAY: "Primate colour vision is often argued to have evolved partly for spotting ripe fruit and things that stand out against foliage. Colour is a detection system before it is a decoration system."
Source: Mylonas, Week 4 Colour (LDSCI5209) p5, wildlifesos.org.

slides.name: 23 · Full picture

params.text: Colour finds it for you. Unless you are a deer
With two cone types, a deer sees this orange as green · Fennell et al. (2019)

slides.notes:
45 s.
The deer: orange works as camouflage because deer are dichromats (Fennell et al., 2019, J. R. Soc. Interface). Plant it now; colour vision deficiency comes back in Section 3, where about 1 in 12 men in the room see a little like the deer.
Source: Mylonas, Week 4 Colour (LDSCI5209) p6, wildlifesos.org.

slides.name: 24 · Predict: which one will be hardest to read?

params.text: Predict: which one will be hardest to read?
Predict: which one will be hardest to read?

A · Lightness only: you can see every shape and edge, but not which fruit is which.

B · Colour only: you know there are oranges and apples, but the edges are gone. Most people find B hardest.

C · Both: the full picture.

slides.notes:
1.5 min. Poll first, results held; then reveal the bars and flip (⇄).
Most predict A. The surprise is B: without lightness there are no edges.
Source: Mylonas, Week 4 Colour (LDSCI5209) p7–9, after Stockman & Brainard (2009).

args.caption: Predict: which one will be hardest to read?
args.facts:
A · Lightness only: you can see every shape and edge, but not which fruit is which.
B · Colour only: you know there are oranges and apples, but the edges are gone. Most people find B hardest.
C · Both: the full picture.

slides.name: 25 · Full picture

params.text: Lightness shows where. Hue shows what.
Remember this split: it becomes the rule for encoding data

slides.notes:
1 min.
SAY: "Lightness gives you shape and edges. Colour gives you identity. Remember this split, because it becomes the rule for encoding data: lightness for how much, hue for which one."

slides.name: 26 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
1 min. Read the three steps aloud and point at the quarters key. Phones out now, joined, before the flash.
SAY: "We’re testing whether colour lets your eye find something without searching. Two seconds isn’t long enough to search, so if you find it, colour did the work." Don’t say yet what changes in round 2.

args.caption: Can you find it in two seconds?

slides.name: 27 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
Click away after two seconds, then ASK: "Hands up: A? B? C? D?" Expect almost everyone on C.
2 s only. SAY: "You get two seconds. Find the red dot." Count two, then click on.
Flashing it, rather than leaving it up, is the point: if colour pops out, two seconds is plenty.

slides.name: 28 · Framed picture
slides.notes: 20 s. SAY: "Same task, same two seconds. One thing changes. Ready?" Then click.

slides.name: 29 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
Click away after two seconds, then hands up again. Expect the room to split: the answer is B.
2 s only. SAY: "Same again. Two seconds." Then click on.

slides.name: 30 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
1.5 min. Recall the two shows of hands: round 1 near-unanimous, round 2 scattered.
ROUND 1, POP-OUT. SAY: "Some features, colour among them, are processed in parallel across your whole field of view. One red dot among grey is found in about the same time however many dots there are. Two seconds is too short to search, so if you found it, colour did the work." (Treisman & Gelade, 1980; Munzner p109: one red item "immediately noticed from a sea of gray ones").
ROUND 2, WHY IT BROKE. SAY: "The red didn’t change. Its surroundings did. Red was now one colour among many, and one dot was an orange-red close to it. Pop-out depends on how different the target is from everything around it." This is similarity, not a harder target: search slows when distractors resemble the target and differ from each other (Duncan & Humphreys, 1989; Munzner p109–110: popout "is not an all-or-nothing phenomenon").
SO WHAT. SAY: "In a chart, give colour to the one thing you want seen first, and keep the rest grey. Colour everything and you highlight nothing." This sets up Start with grey and the Netflix chart later.

args.caption: Colour only highlights when it is scarce

slides.name: 31 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
1.5 min. Why the red dot was so fast. SAY: "Your brain processes colour before you are conscious of looking: an odd colour is found in a fraction of a second, faster than reading. That is why colour is so powerful for highlighting key insights, and why it stops working when everything is coloured."
Fix carried over: the 2025 deck quoted "about 200 milliseconds, faster than reading" without a source. Pre-attentive features such as hue are detected in under about 200–250 ms (Healey & Enns, 2012; Treisman & Gelade, 1980).
Source: 2025 Week 4 deck p16 (brain diagram).

slides.name: 32 · Section · Where does colour come from?
slides.notes: 20 s. From light, to three cones, to three channels in the brain.

slides.name: 33 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
3 min across three clicks.
SAY: "Colour isn’t in the light. Light has wavelengths, and colour is what your brain builds from them." About 120 million rods (night vision, no colour) and about 6 million cones, packed into the fovea.
Source: Mylonas p12–13.

slides.name: 34 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
Three cone types, short, medium and long, each sensitive to its own overlapping band. Curve shapes are simplified; the peaks follow Stockman & Sharpe (2000), about 440, 540 and 565 nm.
Source: Mylonas p14.

slides.name: 35 · Framed picture
slides.notes: SAY: "Light at 580 nm. L answers strongly, M a little less, S almost not at all. Those three numbers are all your brain gets, and it reads that mix as yellow. That is trichromacy. Your screen exploits it: three lights, red, green and blue, are enough to fake every colour."

slides.name: 36 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
2 min.
SAY: "After the cones, the signal is recoded into three opponent channels: light–dark, red–green and blue–yellow. That is why you can’t imagine a reddish green. It is also why the perceptual opposites are red–green and blue–yellow, not the painter’s complementaries; we come back to that."
Lightness carries edges and detail; the two colour channels are coarser (Munzner p220).
Source: Mylonas p17, after Hering (1878/1964).

slides.name: 37 · Colour vision deficiency

params.text:
Deuteranomaly: the M cones are shifted, so reds and greens drift together. The most common form, about 5% of men.

Protanopia: no L cones. Red loses its brightness and turns dark olive.

Tritanopia: no S cones. Blue and yellow are the pair that goes. Rare.

-anomaly means a cone type is shifted; -opia means it is missing.

slides.notes:
1 min. The world first, then the chart on the next slide.
SAY: "Same photograph, four eyes. Deuteranomaly: the M cones are shifted, so reds and greens drift together. Protanopia: no L cones, so red goes dark olive. Tritanopia: no S cones, so blue and yellow are the ones that go." Remember the deer and the tiger: this is what two cone types does.
-anomaly means a cone type is shifted; -opia means it is missing.
Source: 2025 Week 4 deck p15, credited there to The Sun (2017). Your plan suggests replacing that source: a Coblis (color-blindness.com) simulation of any photo does the same job with a better credit.

args.caption: Colour vision deficiency
args.credit: The same parrots, four ways of seeing
args.facts:
Deuteranomaly: the M cones are shifted, so reds and greens drift together. The most common form, about 5% of men.
Protanopia: no L cones. Red loses its brightness and turns dark olive.
Tritanopia: no S cones. Blue and yellow are the pair that goes. Rare.
-anomaly means a cone type is shifted; -opia means it is missing.

slides.name: 38 · The same chart, four ways of seeing it

params.text: The same chart, four ways of seeing it

About 8% of men and 0.5% of women have a colour vision deficiency; rates are highest in people of Northern European descent (Munzner p235).

Most forms affect the red–green channel: deuteranomaly alone is about 5% of men.

-anomaly: a cone type is shifted. -opia: it is missing.

Confusions aren’t only red/green: also red/black, blue/purple, light green/white, brown/green (Munzner p235).

slides.notes:
2.5 min. ASK: "In each panel, which line is North?" In the deuteranopia and protanopia panels North and South merge; in tritanopia, South and East close up.
SAY: "In a lecture hall of 60, expect two or three people to see your red/green chart as one colour, and never ask them to put a hand up."
Flip (⇄) for the numbers. Simulation: Machado, Oliveira & Fernandes (2009), severity 1, as in Week 3’s scales experiment.

args.caption: The same chart, four ways of seeing it
args.facts:
About 8% of men and 0.5% of women have a colour vision deficiency; rates are highest in people of Northern European descent (Munzner p235).
Most forms affect the red–green channel: deuteranomaly alone is about 5% of men.
-anomaly: a cone type is shifted. -opia: it is missing.
Confusions aren’t only red/green: also red/black, blue/purple, light green/white, brown/green (Munzner p235).

slides.name: 39 · Section · Can you trust what you see?

params.text: Can you trust what you see?

slides.notes: 20 s. The same colour can look different. Albers, then a heatmap, then your brain correcting the light.

slides.name: 40 · In order to use colour effectively it is necessary to recognise that it deceives continually.

params.text: In order to use colour effectively it is necessary to recognise that it deceives continually.

slides.notes: 20 s. SAY: "Albers spent a career showing that the same colour looks different depending on its neighbours."

slides.name: 41 · Framed picture
slides.notes: 1 min. Vote with the picture up, show the bars, then click on to the reveal. Most say Left.

slides.name: 42 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
30 s. The bar of the same grey joins the two squares, and the difference disappears.
Source: after Albers (1963) and Mylonas p21–22.

args.caption: One grey. The neighbours changed it

slides.name: 43 · Framed picture
slides.notes: 1.5 min. Vote with the picture up, then show the bars. P sits among dark cells and looks lighter; Q sits among light cells and looks darker. Few say "the same", which is the answer.

args.caption: Which cell holds the higher value: P or Q?

slides.name: 44 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
1.5 min.
SAY: "Your readers aren’t reading colour values. They’re reading colour relative to the neighbourhood. That is why colour is a weak channel for precise comparison, and why position beats colour in Munzner’s ranking."
Munzner p223: on a non-uniform background people tell apart fewer than five lightness steps. The fixes: print the value, use fewer steps, add a cell border. Makeover map B fails exactly here.

slides.name: 45 · Colour constancy

params.text:
One cube sits in yellow light, the other in blue.

Pick a tile on each that looks a different colour from the other. Are they?

slides.notes:
OPTIONAL, 1.5 min with the next slide.
ASK: "One cube sits in yellow light, the other in blue. Pick a tile on each that looks a different colour from the other. Are they?"
Source: Mylonas p25.

args.caption: Colour constancy
args.facts:
One cube sits in yellow light, the other in blue.
Pick a tile on each that looks a different colour from the other. Are they?

slides.name: 46 · The same colour: your brain discounted the light

params.text: The same colour: your brain discounted the light

The joining bar shows the two tiles are the same colour.

Your brain estimates the light falling on each cube and discounts it: colour constancy.

In charts: shading, 3D lighting and tinted overlays change the colours people read.

slides.notes:
OPTIONAL.
SAY: "Your brain tries to discount the lighting. Brilliant for survival, terrible for reading a heatmap under a shaded overlay." Remember the dress from Week 2: that was colour constancy disagreeing with itself. Shading on 3D charts does the same to data colours.
Source: Mylonas p26.

args.caption: The same colour: your brain discounted the light
args.facts:
The joining bar shows the two tiles are the same colour.
Your brain estimates the light falling on each cube and discounts it: colour constancy.
In charts: shading, 3D lighting and tinted overlays change the colours people read.

slides.name: 47 · Section · What is a colour made of?

params.text: What is a colour made of?

slides.notes: 20 s. Three dimensions, and the one that has no order.

slides.name: 48 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
3 min across four clicks.
HUE: which colour family. An identity channel: best for categories (Munzner p224).

slides.name: 49 · Framed picture
slides.notes: LIGHTNESS: how light or dark. A magnitude channel: best for ordered and quantitative data. People reliably order it.

slides.name: 50 · Framed picture
slides.notes: SATURATION: how vivid or grey. Also a magnitude channel, but weak: about three distinguishable steps (Munzner p223).

slides.name: 51 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
All three.
SAY: "This table is the whole lecture in miniature. Hue answers what kind. Lightness answers how much."

slides.name: 52 · Hue: the colour family

params.text:
A different hue is a different family: use it for categories.

Decreasing saturation keeps the family but greys it.

A darker value keeps the family but deepens it: use that for order.

slides.notes:
1 min. Your 2025 diagram of the three dimensions on one hue. SAY: "Hue says which family. Saturation and darkness stay inside the family, so they can say how much."
Source: 2025 Week 4 deck p19.

args.caption: Hue: the colour family
args.facts:
A different hue is a different family: use it for categories.
Decreasing saturation keeps the family but greys it.
A darker value keeps the family but deepens it: use that for order.

slides.name: 53 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
2 min. The first of two colour models you already know that mislead you; HSL is next.
SAY: "The wheel on the left is the art-class model, built for mixing paint. On the right is what your eye does with full-strength hues: yellow nearly white, blue nearly black, and red and green on one channel." The painter’s complementary pair, red–green, is the pair 1 in 12 men can’t separate.
ASK: "If equal steps round the wheel looked equally different, would yellow and blue be this far apart in lightness?"
Harmonies (complementary, triadic…) come back in Build, as a tool for choosing hues within a colour map.
Fix carried over: the 2025 deck’s analogous example read "Blue-Blue-Green-Green"; it is blue, blue-green, green.
Source: 2025 Week 4 deck p9.

args.caption: The painter’s wheel vs your eye

slides.name: 54 · Framed picture
slides.notes: 2 min across two clicks. Every colour picker has an L slider; these six are all at 50%. ASK: "Are they equally light?" Then click to print them in greyscale.

slides.name: 55 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
The greyscale row is each colour’s CIE lightness. HSL says all six are 50%; your eye says yellow is 97 and blue is 32.
SAY: "This is exactly why a rainbow scale creates false bright bands around yellow and cyan." ASK: "If yellow sits in the middle of your scale, where will the eye think the peak is?"

slides.name: 56 · Framed picture
slides.notes: 1.5 min. Hands up, or call out: take three or four different orders from the room. Expect no agreement. The rainbow order (red, yellow, green, blue, purple: C, E, A, D, B) is a convention you learnt, not something you see.

args.caption: Put these in order, least to most

slides.name: 57 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
1.5 min. Lightest to darkest: B, D, A, E, C. Almost everyone agrees.
SAY: "Everyone agrees on the second ordering and nobody agrees on the first. That is the empirical case against rainbow scales for quantitative data." (Munzner p224, Figure 10.5.)

slides.name: 58 · Section · What jobs can colour do in a chart?

params.text: What jobs can colour do in a chart?

slides.notes: 20 s. Label, measure, highlight, mean; what happens when the jobs are swapped; then the three families of colour map the jobs become.

slides.name: 59 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
2 min across five clicks, one job lit per click. This is where the vocabulary pays off.
LABEL: separate categories. Hue is an identity channel (the last section): different hues say different things, with equal status.

args.caption: Four jobs colour does in a chart

slides.name: 60 · Framed picture
slides.notes: MEASURE: show magnitude. Lightness is a magnitude channel: everyone ordered the greys, nobody agreed on the hues. So darker reads as more.

args.caption: Four jobs colour does in a chart

slides.name: 61 · Framed picture
slides.notes: HIGHLIGHT: direct attention. One colour against grey: remember the red dot, it only works when colour is scarce.

args.caption: Four jobs colour does in a chart

slides.name: 62 · Framed picture
slides.notes: MEAN: carry associations. Warming stripes: blue cold, red hot. Also danger, loss, brand. Meaning is learned, so it varies by audience.

args.caption: Four jobs colour does in a chart

slides.name: 63 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
All four.
SAY: "Most bad charts mix these jobs up. They use label colours to show measure data, as the fly-the-nest chart did."

args.caption: Four jobs colour does in a chart

slides.name: 64 · Framed picture
slides.notes: 2.5 min across three slides. ASK: "Six years of hires. What is the story?" Nobody can say: every line shouts.

slides.name: 65 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
SAY: "Same chart, grey first, then colour for the one line with a story: 2020, when lockdown emptied March and April and hires jumped in May." This completes the Highlight job and pays off the red dot (slide 24): colour works when it is scarce.
Data: TfL daily cycle hires, monthly totals.

slides.name: 66 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
1 min. SAY: "Professional newsrooms often build charts in grey first and add colour only where they want the eye to go. The Times keeps a limited palette with consistent meanings." ASK: "In the City Intelligence guidelines, what is grey for, and what is blue for?"
Source: The Times (2021) and data.london.gov.uk City Intelligence guidelines, 2025 deck p18 and p24.

slides.name: 67 · City Intelligence data design guidelines

params.text:
Review the guidelines: colour scheme, text and layout.

What is grey for? What is blue for?

Which colours carry the data, and which carry the context?

How do the same rules work on a light and a dark background?

slides.notes:
3 min. The GLA’s own chart guidelines for London data. In pairs, review them for colour scheme, text and layout (the 2025 deck’s activity), then take answers.
Expected: grey for context and axes, one strong colour for the point, the same styling on light and dark grounds, and consistent titles and labels.
Source: data.london.gov.uk/blog/city-intelligence-data-design-guidelines, 2025 deck p24.

args.caption: City Intelligence data design guidelines
args.facts:
Review the guidelines: colour scheme, text and layout.
What is grey for? What is blue for?
Which colours carry the data, and which carry the context?
How do the same rules work on a light and a dark background?

slides.name: 68 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
2.5 min. The data behind Case C, twelve countries. It has two things to show: a category (region) and a quantity (age leaving home).
LEFT, RIGHT CHANNEL. Label: four distinct hues, so four regions that are different and equal. Measure: one lightness ramp, so darker is older and Southern Europe jumps out without the legend.
RIGHT, CHANNELS SWAPPED. Label with shades of one hue and the regions look ranked: is Southern "more" than Nordic? Measure with rainbow hues and nobody can say whether orange is older than green without reading the legend. That second panel is exactly what Case C did.
ASK: "Cover the legends. Which panels still work?" The two left ones do: hue says which, lightness says how much.
Data: Eurostat 2022, average age young people leave the parental household, values as printed in Case C.

slides.name: 69 · Section · Which colour map for which data?

params.text: Which colour map for which data?

slides.notes: 20 s. The jobs become three families. We see all three, then go through them one at a time with real charts.

slides.name: 70 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
2 min. The overview. The jobs become three families: MEASURE becomes sequential, MEASURE FROM A MIDDLE becomes diverging, LABEL becomes categorical. Week 2 named them; now they have their reasons. We classify five datasets, then take each family in turn.
Source: Brewer (1994); Harrower & Brewer (2003); Munzner Fig. 10.6.

slides.name: 71 · Framed picture
slides.notes: 2 min. Predict first: hands up for each card, S, D or C? Let satisfaction (2) and Brexit (3) split the room and take one reason from each side. Don’t reveal yet: we check these predictions after the three families.

args.caption: Classify these: sequential, diverging or categorical?

slides.name: 72 · Framed picture
slides.notes: SEQUENTIAL, in depth. Low to high: lightness does the work and hue may shift a little. Rainfall, income, density. Then a real map to judge.

slides.name: 73 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
1.5 min.
SAY: "On the left, a reader has to learn the legend: orange means low. On the right, darker means more, and nobody needs the legend to see the pattern. With a good sequential scale the legend is for precision; with a bad one it is needed just for meaning."
Source: Datawrapper blog (Lisa Charlotte Muth), 2025 deck p31.

slides.name: 74 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
1.5 min. ASK: "Where is the heaviest rain?" On A the eye goes to the bright yellow band; on B to the darkest green. Then: "Which one could you read in greyscale?"
Source: hellerweather.com, “Data visualization and the overused rainbow color table”, via Mylonas p39.

slides.name: 75 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
3 min across two clicks. Real data: the TfL 2024 heatmap from slide 3 in three colour maps. The line under each is its CIE lightness from low to high.
AGAINST THE RAINBOW (jet): false boundaries at yellow and cyan, lightness up then down, and it fails for colour-blind readers (Borland & Taylor, 2007).
VIRIDIS (van der Walt & Smith, 2015): built in a perceptually uniform space; lightness climbs steadily, so it survives greyscale and colour blindness.
TURBO (Google, 2019): keeps the rainbow’s many nameable hues with smoother lightness, but is still dark at both ends, so not for order.

slides.name: 76 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
Greyscale. Only viridis still runs dark to light. In jet, the busiest summer days and the quietest winter Sundays come out similar greys, because jet is dark at both ends.
ASK: "Weather presenters still use rainbows. Habit, or is there a task where a rainbow helps?" Possible answers: naming bands ("the red area"), reading exact values off a legend, familiarity.

slides.name: 77 · Common mistakes: the rainbow

params.text:
The rainbow has no inherent order: hue is an identity channel.

Yellow looks brighter than blue even at the same value, so it makes false peaks.

Colour-blind readers lose whole bands of it.

slides.notes:
1.5 min. The rainbow wheel as two colour-blind readers see it: whole bands merge.
SAY: "Rainbow has no inherent order; yellow looks brighter than blue at the same value; and colour-blind readers can’t separate parts of it." Three problems, three earlier lessons: the ordering test, why HSL lies, and the parrots.
Source: 2025 Week 4 deck p17.

args.caption: Common mistakes: the rainbow
args.facts:
The rainbow has no inherent order: hue is an identity channel.
Yellow looks brighter than blue even at the same value, so it makes false peaks.
Colour-blind readers lose whole bands of it.

slides.name: 78 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
3 min. Same data, same colours, three different stories.
EQUAL INTERVAL: Croatia sits alone in the darkest class and most countries look middling. QUANTILE: a fifth in each class, so small differences look as big as large ones. NATURAL BREAKS: classes follow the gaps in the data, so clusters stand out.
SAY: "The bins are an editorial decision." ASK: "Which version would a campaign about young people stuck at home choose? Which would a government choose?"
Altair: scale=alt.Scale(type='quantile') or 'quantize' (equal interval); natural breaks need thresholds computed first (type='threshold').
Data: Eurostat 2022 as printed in Case C, EU-27 average left out.

slides.name: 79 · Framed picture
slides.notes: DIVERGING, in depth. Two directions from a meaningful midpoint. SAY: "Is the midpoint meaningful? Zero, average and 50% are. The median of whatever you happened to collect usually isn’t." Then a survey chart and the warming stripes.

slides.name: 80 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
1.5 min.
SAY: "Likert data is ordered and has a neutral middle: the textbook diverging case. In the not-ideal version, agree and disagree are similar teals that the eye groups together, which is semantically backwards."
Source: Datawrapper blog, 2025 deck p32.

slides.name: 81 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
3 min. The UK, 1884–2025: one stripe per year. The 1961–2010 average is the boundary between blue and red, and the scale spans ±3 standard deviations of 1901–2000 temperatures (showyourstripes.info). A diverging scale with no axes, no numbers and no legend, shared millions of times.
ASK: "Is this good data visualisation? What does it gain by removing everything? What does it lose?" Then: "Would it work with a rainbow scale?"
It pits communication against precision. Blue to red works because the midpoint (the average) is meaningful and lightness is symmetrical.
Image: Ed Hawkins, University of Reading, showyourstripes.info, CC BY 4.0. UK data: Met Office (HadUK).

slides.name: 82 · Framed picture
slides.notes: CATEGORICAL, in depth. Distinct groups with no order: hue, equal status, at most 6–12. Then a bar chart to judge, two rules that disagree, and what mark size does.

slides.name: 83 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
1.5 min.
SAY: "Shades of one blue imply an order that doesn’t exist. Is Egypt less than Pakistan? Different hues say different things, equal status." Same lesson as One dataset, two jobs.
Source: Datawrapper blog, 2025 deck p30. The two treemap pairs (p33–34) are optional extras.

slides.name: 84 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
2.5 min. Both rules appear in respected sources, and your own 2025 deck states both (p35 and p36). Vote first, then click to print both palettes in greyscale.
Rule A palette: CIE L* 68 for all six. Rule B: L* from 35 to 88.

args.caption: Two respected rules. Which is right?

slides.name: 85 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
The greyscale row settles part of it: Rule A’s six colours are one grey; Rule B’s stay apart.
RESOLUTION: it is a trade-off. Rule A protects equal salience; Rule B protects discriminability, especially for colour-blind readers, greyscale printing and small marks. In practice: vary lightness modestly and use direct labels.
Bonus: the 2025 deck’s "nominal" example swatches don’t actually have constant lightness either.

args.caption: Two respected rules. Which is right?

slides.name: 86 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
2 min. ASK: "In each row, can you still count five colours?"
SAY: "Colours that are distinct as large areas merge as small marks. The colour difference needed to tell two apart grows as marks shrink (Szafir, 2018). The rule of thumb: muted colours for big areas, saturated colours for small marks." The last row is the fix.
Munzner p224: use bright, saturated colours for small regions and pastels for large backgrounds. This is why the label job has a limit.

slides.name: 87 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
2.5 min. Real data: TfL monthly hires, one line per year. ASK: "On the left, which line is 2020?" Nobody can say without hunting through the legend.
SAY: "Roughly 6–12 distinguishable categorical colours, including background and default colours, and fewer for small marks (Munzner, Ch. 10). You will sometimes hear the 7-colour rule, borrowed from Miller’s 7±2. That was about memory, not colour."
With 15 categories: group them, highlight two or three and grey the rest, use small multiples, or label directly. The right panel does the second and the last.
Fix carried over: the 2025 deck’s 7-colour slide had the speaker note "Explain that…" left on it.

args.caption: How many colours can people tell apart?

slides.name: 88 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
OPTIONAL, 2 min with the next. SAY: "The better version maps darkness to size: redundant encoding. It reinforces the message, but it spends a channel." ASK: "Could colour encode something else, such as growth rate? When is redundancy a virtue, and when is it waste?"
Source: Datawrapper blog, 2025 deck p33.

slides.name: 89 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
OPTIONAL. The second pair: the same question.
Source: Datawrapper blog, 2025 deck p34.

slides.name: 90 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
All three again.
SAY: "The question isn’t which looks nicer. It’s what the data’s structure says: low to high, two ways from a middle, or different with no order." Next: the palette types designers use, judged by these jobs.

args.caption: Three families of colour map · summary

slides.name: 91 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
2 min. Back to the predictions from the start of this part. Each answer, and why two are debatable.
SAY: "Notice that the answer depends on the task, not just the data. That is Munzner’s abstraction level at work."
Fix carried over: the 2025 deck labelled the Brexit example "diverging" without qualification.

slides.name: 92 · Section · What does colour say?
slides.notes: 20 s. Colour carries meaning before anyone reads a label: matched to concepts, light or dark, cultural, branded.

slides.name: 93 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
1.5 min. SAY: "Warm and cool colours sit on opposite sides of the wheel. Warm colours read as energy, urgency and attention; cool colours as calm, trust and professionalism. Brands lean on this: look at which sectors pick blue." Then add the caution that the next slides develop: these are associations, not laws.
Source: 2025 Week 4 deck p13 and p25.

slides.name: 94 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
1.5 min. Our own example after the infographic. Real data, TfL 2024 monthly hires, drawn twice. ASK: "Which one looks like a problem?" Most say the red one, though the numbers are identical.
SAY: "Warm colours pull attention and read as urgency; cool colours read as calm. Neither is wrong, but the colour is making a claim the data doesn’t."

args.caption: Warm or cool: does colour change the message?

slides.name: 95 · Colours by culture

params.text:
Colour meanings aren’t universal.

Red means danger in many Western contexts, and luck and prosperity in China.

For a global audience, research your colour choices, and let labels fix the meaning.

slides.notes:
1.5 min. SAY: "Colour meanings aren’t universal. Red means luck and prosperity in China but danger in Western contexts. If you’re creating visualisations for global audiences, research your colour choices."
This popular chart is a starting point, not evidence: it generalises whole regions. The next slide is about how much of this research supports.
Source: 2025 Week 4 deck p26.

args.caption: Colours by culture
args.facts:
Colour meanings aren’t universal.
Red means danger in many Western contexts, and luck and prosperity in China.
For a global audience, research your colour choices, and let labels fix the meaning.

slides.name: 96 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
1.5 min. An illustrative seat map, the same picture for two audiences. SAY: "In London, red is Labour, the left. In Washington, red is the Republicans, the right. Same map, opposite story."
ASK: "What does your chart need so nobody reads it backwards?" A legend or direct labels that say what each colour means. The seat counts are invented; the conventions are real.

slides.name: 97 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
1.5 min. SAY: "Same data, opposite colours. A Chinese investor reading a Western chart, or the reverse, may get the story backwards. This is the strongest data-vis example of cultural colour meaning."
Also: red is Labour in London and Republican in Washington. The price series is illustrative.

slides.name: 98 · Colour psychology: handle with care

params.text:
These associations are popular claims, rarely cited.

Across about 30 nations, colour–emotion links are broadly shared but shaped by language and place (Jonauskaite et al., 2020).

Treat them as hypotheses to test with your audience, and let context fix the meaning.

slides.notes:
2 min. Labelled POPULAR CLAIMS on purpose.
SAY: "Infographics like this are everywhere and rarely cite evidence. A large study across about 30 nations (Jonauskaite et al., 2020) found colour–emotion associations are broadly shared, red with love and anger for example, but also shaped by language and geography. So they are neither universal laws nor purely cultural: treat them as hypotheses to test with your audience."
ASK: "Red means danger and love in Western culture. How does a reader know which you mean?" Context.
Source: geeksforgeeks.org via the 2025 deck p27.

args.caption: Colour psychology: handle with care
args.facts:
These associations are popular claims, rarely cited.
Across about 30 nations, colour–emotion links are broadly shared but shaped by language and place (Jonauskaite et al., 2020).
Treat them as hypotheses to test with your audience, and let context fix the meaning.

slides.name: 99 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
2 min. Real data: TfL monthly hires against 2023. ASK: "In the left chart, which months went badly?" February and September look like failures, but a fall in bike hires isn’t a failure unless your story says so.
SAY: "Traffic-light colours add a verdict. A neutral pair like blue and orange says only up and down. Save alarm colours for data that is alarming." It also fixes red–green for colour-blind readers.

slides.name: 100 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
2 min. SAY: "Readers interpret charts faster when colours match concepts (Lin et al., 2013). Use meaning when it exists, and don’t fight it."
ASK: "What’s the natural colour for the Liberal Democrats? For temperature? For profit?"
The fruit numbers are illustrative: the point is the colour.

args.caption: Use the colour the concept already has

slides.name: 101 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
2 min. Same TfL heatmap, same scale, two backgrounds. ASK: "Which months were busiest?" On white, almost everyone points at the dark summer cells. On black, some will point at the light cells.
SAY: "People tend to read darker as more, the dark-is-more bias, but on dark backgrounds the expectation can flip (Schloss et al., 2019). The right direction depends on your background."

slides.name: 102 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
2 min. SAY: "The NYT has a huge flexible palette that covers every use case. The FT and The Economist use very few hues, with shades of each. Fewer hues means a recognisable brand, but harder categorical charts."
ASK: "If you designed for the FT, how would you show seven political parties?" (Shades of a few hues, labels, or position rather than colour.)
Source: Datawrapper blog, “Colors for data vis style guides”, 2025 deck p20–21.

slides.name: 103 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
1.5 min. SAY: "In the line chart, brand colour does the storytelling: the black and red lines are the story and everything else recedes. In the Statista chart, light versus dark orange encodes 2016 versus 2017, a small ordered use of lightness."
Fix carried over: the 2025 deck had stray text about sequential schemes on this slide.
Source: 2025 deck p22–23 (Statista).

slides.name: 104 · Section · Who can’t read your chart?
slides.notes: 20 s. Accessibility, opened by the colour vision deficiency chart from Part 2.

slides.name: 105 · Framed picture
slides.notes: 1 min. The chart from Part 2 again. ASK: "Now you know the jobs and the colour maps: what would you change so every panel works?" Different lightness, direct labels, and no red–green pair. The next slides turn that into rules and tests.

slides.name: 106 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
2 min across two clicks. Weekdays against Sundays in red and green, with only a legend. The inset is the same chart as a deuteranope sees it: two near-identical lines.
WCAG 2.x: 1.4.1 Use of Color (colour must not be the only way information is conveyed); 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast (graphical objects 3:1 against neighbours); 1.4.3 Contrast (text 4.5:1).

slides.name: 107 · Framed picture
slides.notes: The fix: dark solid against light dashed, labelled at the end of each line. It now works in greyscale, for colour-blind readers, and without a legend.

slides.name: 108 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
1.5 min. Four ways to say it twice: direct labels, line style or shape, lightness differences, annotation.
SAY: "Every one of these also helps readers with perfect colour vision. Accessible design is usually just better design."

slides.name: 109 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
1.5 min. GREYSCALE: desaturate it; does it still work? COLOUR BLINDNESS: in Chrome DevTools open Rendering → Emulate vision deficiencies, or use Coblis.
SAY: "This room’s projector is a third test. The pale end of your sequential scale may have just vanished."

slides.name: 110 · Section · How do you build it?
slides.notes: 20 s. Tools, harmonies as a way to pick hues within a colour map, and Altair.

slides.name: 111 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
5 min with the activity. ColorBrewer for maps (with colour-blind and print filters); Colorgorical for categorical palettes; chroma.js for custom ramps with lightness correction and a CVD check; Adobe Color for harmonies and its accessibility tab; the Stanford colour-name analyser to check categories have distinct names.
The hands-on comes after the palette types: the Palette lab uses ColorBrewer, Adobe Color and chroma.js.
Check: Colorgorical appears at vrl.cs.brown.edu/color and vrl-v2.cs.brown.edu/color; confirm which resolves.
Source: 2025 deck p37–40; Mylonas p41–43.

slides.name: 112 · Six palette types

params.text:
Complementary: opposite hues. Strong contrast.

Analogous: neighbouring hues. Calm, close together.

Monochromatic: one hue, lighter and darker.

Split: one hue and the two neighbours of its opposite.

Triadic: three evenly spaced hues.

Square: four evenly spaced hues.

All six are defined on the painter’s wheel. The next slides test each on data.

slides.notes:
1 min. The six harmonies designers learn: monochromatic, analogous, complementary, split-complementary, triadic, square. They are defined on the painter’s colour wheel and they make palettes pleasing. The question for us is what each one is for when the colours carry data.
Source: 2025 Week 4 deck p10, figma.com/resource-library/types-of-color-palettes.

args.caption: Six palette types
args.facts:
Complementary: opposite hues. Strong contrast.
Analogous: neighbouring hues. Calm, close together.
Monochromatic: one hue, lighter and darker.
Split: one hue and the two neighbours of its opposite.
Triadic: three evenly spaced hues.
Square: four evenly spaced hues.
All six are defined on the painter’s wheel. The next slides test each on data.

slides.name: 113 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
6 min: bird’s-eye, one zoom per type on real data, then bird’s-eye again.
BIRD’S-EYE first: let the room scan all six for ten seconds. ASK: "Which of these would you use to show a profit and loss?" Then zoom into each.

args.caption: Six palette types, six data jobs

slides.name: 114 · Framed picture
slides.notes: MONOCHROMATIC → MEASURE. One hue from light to dark: the TfL hires heatmap from slide 3. The safest sequential scale: lightness carries the order, nothing competes.

slides.name: 115 · Framed picture
slides.notes: ANALOGOUS → MEASURE. Neighbouring hues, yellow through green to blue, on the Case C ages. It works only because lightness climbs with it (this is ColorBrewer YlGnBu). Neighbouring hues at equal lightness would lose the order.

slides.name: 116 · Framed picture
slides.notes: COMPLEMENTARY → DIVERGE. Opposites meet at a middle: months where hires rose against 2023 in blue, fell in orange. Perfect for up/down, profit/loss, agree/disagree. But the painter’s classic complementary pair is red–green, the one pair 1 in 12 men can’t separate. Use blue–orange.

slides.name: 117 · Framed picture
slides.notes: SPLIT-COMPLEMENTARY → HIGHLIGHT. One hue leads (2024 in blue) and the two neighbours of its opposite stay pale (2022, 2023). The story is the blue line; the others are context. Remember: colour highlights only when it is scarce.

slides.name: 118 · Framed picture
slides.notes: TRIADIC → LABEL. Three evenly spaced hues for three equal, unrelated categories: weekday, Saturday and Sunday hires. Check they also differ in lightness so they survive greyscale and colour blindness: here red, gold and blue do.

slides.name: 119 · Framed picture
slides.notes: SQUARE → LABEL. Four evenly spaced hues for four categories: mean age by region. That is near the useful limit for small marks (Munzner: about six or seven hues for small, separate marks), so label the bars rather than rely on a legend.

slides.name: 120 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
All six.
SAY: "Harmony rules make palettes pleasing. They don’t make them readable. Pick the palette by the data’s job: measure with one hue or neighbours that climb in lightness, diverge with two opposites, label with evenly spaced hues, highlight with one hue against quiet ones."
Data: TfL daily cycle hires (London Datastore), lessons/tfl-daily-cycle-hires.xlsx; Eurostat 2022 as printed in Case C.

args.caption: Six palette types, six data jobs · summary

slides.name: 121 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
1 min to brief, 8 min of work. Pairs, laptops or phones. Point at the three URLs.
Built from the 2025 deck’s own activities: ColorBrewer 2.0 (p37), Adobe Color with a student account (p39) and the chroma.js palette helper (p40).
Adobe hint from the 2025 deck: complementary colours give strong contrast but can vibrate or clash; analogous feel harmonious but may lack contrast; triadic balance the two.

args.caption: Palette lab: pick it, harmonise it, test it

slides.name: 122 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
8 min on the clock. Number pairs off 1–5 around the room. Circulate: check each pair has written its family down before opening ColorBrewer.
Expected: 1 diverging (e.g. RdBu, PuOr), 2 sequential or diverging (Blues, or PuOr if 5 is neutral), 3 diverging around 50%, 4 diverging (RdBu reversed: blue cold, red warm), 5 categorical (Set2, Dark2; check lightness varies).

slides.name: 123 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
3 min. Two or three pairs share screens and read the sentence. Pick at least one pair whose palette failed the test: the failure is the best teaching moment.
They keep the hex codes for the Lab 4 house palette.

slides.name: 124 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
3 min. SAY: "The data type suffix, :Q, :O or :N, makes Altair pick sensible default scales. That is attribute typing from last week, paying off." "domainMid is how you guarantee a diverging midpoint sits where it should." Natural breaks need thresholds computed first (type='threshold').
Lab 4 uses all five.

slides.name: 125 · Section · Can you fix it?
slides.notes: 20 s. Back to the three parked cases, then the checklist and the close.

slides.name: 126 · Framed picture
slides.notes: 6 min. Back to the three parked cases. Groups take one case each and answer three questions: data type and task; colour-map family and why; one accessibility improvement.

slides.name: 127 · Framed picture
slides.notes: 3 min. CASE A: normalise by population, then a single-hue sequential scale, or drop colour and keep the labels. CASE B: make the sea neutral grey, give the data a hue unlike the basemap, label every bin, say what white means. CASE C: a sequential scale for the age bins, or abandon colour and sort the countries as a bar chart. Sorting is the strongest fix.

args.caption: Fix the opening maps: our answers

slides.name: 128 · Framed picture
slides.notes: 1.5 min. The take-away: eight questions, each tied to the part of today that taught it. It is also the Lab 4 rubric.
